term: "Mean Absolute Error (MAE)"

difficulty: "Beginner"

## Simple explanation

Mean Absolute Error (MAE) measures the typical size of prediction errors
without regard to whether predictions are too high or too low. It averages
the absolute distance between each prediction and its true value.

## Technical explanation

For $n$ observations with targets $y_i$ and predictions $\hat{y}_i$:

$$
\operatorname{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-\hat{y}_i|
$$

MAE is measured in the same units as the target. Absolute error gives each
unit of deviation a linear penalty, making MAE less sensitive to large
outliers than squared-error metrics.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

MAE is easy to interpret when errors have a meaningful unit, such as minutes,
dollars, or degrees. It is often useful alongside other metrics because it
does not reveal the direction of errors and can hide subgroup performance.

## How it works

For every example, subtract the prediction from the observed value, take the
absolute value, and average the results. Lower MAE means smaller average
absolute errors on the evaluated examples.

## Practical example

If a delivery-time model has absolute errors of 2, 4, and 6 minutes on three
deliveries, its MAE is 4 minutes. This gives a direct description of the
average miss size.

## Common misconceptions

- MAE does not indicate whether a model systematically overpredicts or underpredicts.
- A low MAE on a test set does not guarantee low error for every group or future period.
- MAE and mean squared error rank models differently when their error patterns differ.
